title: XRP bug, stablecoin surge, and overdue STR quality fixes
summary: A patched decade-old XRP Ledger vulnerability, a Visa forecast of 1.2 billion stablecoin users in APAC, and two overdue HKMA obligations land on the same day. Alex and Jordan argue about what the XRP disclosure really means for VASP compliance, and whether the stablecoin forecast is a compliance warning or just noise.
script:
JORDAN: Let me put something to you directly, Alex. We have a patched vulnerability in the XRP Ledger that could have allowed someone to mint billions of dollars in XRP from nothing, and the industry response so far seems to be relief that it was caught. I am not relieved.

ALEX: I read that very differently. The patch is actually the good-news part of the story. The fact that the XRP Ledger's developer community identified and closed a decade-old flaw before it was exploited is exactly the kind of protocol-level resilience that supervisors say they want to see from distributed ledger networks. This is AML Agents Briefing for Sunday the eleventh of October, 2026.

JORDAN: I hear you, but here is where I push back. The question for compliance purposes is not whether the patch worked. The question is: during the period that vulnerability was live, could a bad actor have known about it and used it silently? Arbitrary token creation is not just a market integrity problem. It is a transaction-monitoring problem. If XRP could have been conjured from nothing, how confident are you in the historical ledger data your know-your-transaction systems relied on?

ALEX: That is a fair challenge, and I think it is the right question for VASP compliance officers to be asking their technology teams right now. The disclosure was published by CoinDesk on the tenth of October, so you have a clear date to anchor a lookback exercise. But I would caution against overcorrecting. There is no reported evidence of exploitation. A patched vulnerability with no confirmed exploitation is a very different risk posture than an active incident.

JORDAN: Agreed on the calibration, but "no confirmed exploitation" is not the same as "no exploitation." If you are the MLRO at a virtual asset service provider operating under MAS Notice PSN02 or under AUSTRAC's digital currency exchange registration, your board expects you to have a view on this before they ask. My action for listeners is this: before the end of this week, ask your blockchain analytics vendor specifically whether their XRP transaction-monitoring logic flags anomalous token creation events, and if the answer is unclear, escalate that to your chief technology officer in writing. You want a documented response to a documented question.

ALEX: That is a concrete point. Moving on, the Visa survey is the item I want to spend time on because I think the industry is reading it too commercially. The projection that approximately 1.2 billion Asia-Pacific consumers could be using stablecoins by 2031 is, in supervisory terms, a sizing estimate for an unmonitored payment corridor at significant scale.

JORDAN: I am less alarmed than you are, actually, which is a reversal of our usual positions. A Visa survey forecasting consumer appetite five years out is not a regulatory obligation today. Financial intelligence units across the region have known stablecoin exposure is growing. MAS has been consulting on the stablecoin regulatory framework since 2023 and has issued a framework for single-currency stablecoins pegged to the Singapore dollar. Bank Negara Malaysia has its own digital asset licensing track. The supervisory infrastructure is not standing still.

ALEX: I take the point on Singapore and Malaysia, but 1.2 billion consumers is not a number that existing stablecoin AML frameworks were sized to handle. The Egmont Group and the Financial Action Task Force have both flagged, in their guidance on virtual assets, that transaction monitoring at the retail stablecoin layer remains one of the weakest points in the global AML architecture. If that forecast is even directionally correct, the gap between projected volume and current monitoring capacity is a supervisory problem now, not in 2031.

JORDAN: That I agree with. And the read-across for practitioners is specific. If you are the head of financial crime at a bank that is partnering with, or considering partnering with, a stablecoin issuer or a payment aggregator using stablecoins on the backend, now is the time to be pressure-testing whether your customer due diligence and transaction monitoring controls were designed to handle stablecoin flows at any meaningful volume. Do not wait for a thematic review letter.

ALEX: On a related note, the Robinhood Chain transaction decline is worth a brief mention. A drop of more than 40% in transaction volume on a single network creates its own compliance dynamic. When liquidity thins on a chain, the population of remaining active wallets becomes easier to surveil in some respects, but the risk profile of that remaining population can shift. Compliance officers monitoring activity on Robinhood Chain should be reviewing whether their alert thresholds, set when volumes were higher, still make sense at current levels.

JORDAN: Good point. Threshold calibration is one of those maintenance tasks that gets deferred when everything else is urgent. Put it on this quarter's tuning review.

ALEX: Before we close, I want to land on the obligations, because there are two that matter this week. The first is the HKMA annual AML and combating the financing of terrorism self-assessment return, which covers customer due diligence, ongoing monitoring, sanctions screening, suspicious transaction report filing, training, governance, and independent audit. If you are at an HKMA-authorised institution and that return is not submitted, you are already overdue. The second is the HKMA STR quality thematic review from the fourth quarter of 2025. Deficiency letters went to roughly 25% of the authorised institution population earlier this year. If your institution received one, closure of those findings is a live obligation right now.

JORDAN: On the STR quality piece, I want to be specific about what "closure" means in practice because this is where institutions sometimes fall short. It is not enough to tell the HKMA you have updated your suspicious transaction report template. You need to be able to show, with a sample of reports filed since the deficiency letter, that the narrative quality has actually improved. That means a documented quality assurance process, reviewer sign-off records, and ideally a thematic summary your compliance committee has seen. If your institution received a deficiency letter and you cannot show all three of those things today, that is your priority for this week, above everything else we have discussed.

ALEX: And for Singapore-based listeners, the quarterly suspicious transaction report governance review under MAS Notice 626 is also in scope. Completeness, timeliness, escalation effectiveness, and reconciliation of STRO acknowledgements. If that review was due in Q3 and has not been documented, get it done and dated before your next risk committee.

JORDAN: The through-line across all of today's items is the same one it always is. The obligation calendar does not wait for you to finish worrying about the XRP patch. Both things are on your desk at once. That is the job.

ALEX: The full obligation register, source links, and supporting references for everything we have covered today are at amlagents dot streamlit dot app. We will be back tomorrow with whatever the week decides to throw at us. See you then.
